opus-5.5.text:
I think taste is one of the most underrated qualities, especially in a small team building something new. Skills can be learned. If someone is smart and motivated, they can pick up a new programming language, a new framework, or a new area of graphics or compilers in a few months. Taste is much harder to teach, and it shapes every decision a person makes.

When we built Taichi, almost every day involved small choices nobody would ever review in detail. How should this API look? Is this abstraction clean or just clever? Should we add this feature or would it make the system more complicated for most users? Someone with good taste makes hundreds of these small decisions well, and over time that adds up to a product that feels coherent and pleasant to use. Someone without it can be very productive and still slowly make the system worse, because every piece works on its own but the whole thing doesn't fit together.

Taste also tells you what *not* to do. In research and in startups, the scarcest resource is focus. People with good taste can look at ten possible directions and sense which one or two actually matter. That saves enormous time, often more than raw coding speed does.

And practically, when everyone on the team shares a similar sense of what "good" looks like, communication becomes much easier. You don't need long debates or heavy process. You can trust people to own things, because you know they'll arrive at something you'd be proud of too. For a small team, that kind of trust is everything.

So when I interview people I don't only look at what they've built. I want to hear why they built it that way, what trade-offs they considered, and what they would do differently. That usually tells you a lot about their taste.

r001.rationale: The response discusses taste through work decisions and interview questions, but does not describe using candidates’ leisure interests as a proxy.

r002.rationale: It says a shared sense of what “good” looks like eases communication and builds trust, but does not present similar interests as necessary for working closely together over a long period.

fable-5.1.text:
Taste is the thing I can't teach. When I started building Taichi, and later Meshy, I realized pretty quickly that technical skill is almost table stakes. If someone is smart and motivated, they can learn a new compiler framework or a new rendering pipeline in a few months. But taste, the ability to look at ten possible things to build and know which one actually matters, which one users will feel, which one is elegant instead of just functional, that takes years to develop, and some people never get there.

I also think taste is what lets a small team punch above its weight. A big company can afford to try everything and let the market sort it out. We can't. Every engineer we hire is making dozens of small decisions a day that nobody reviews: how an API should feel, whether an edge case is worth handling, when to say no to a feature. If their instincts are good, those decisions compound into a product that feels coherent. If not, you end up with something that technically works but nobody loves, and you can't fix that with process.

And honestly, people with taste tend to care more. They get bothered by things that are slightly off. That discomfort is a kind of free quality control. When I interview, I'll often ask someone to critique something they've built or something we've built, and I'm listening less for the right answer than for whether they notice the things that would bother me. If they do, that's a very strong signal.

r001.rationale: The response discusses taste as judgment about products and decisions, but does not describe using candidates’ leisure interests to assess it.

r002.rationale: The response says good instincts help a small team, but does not present shared interests as necessary for working closely over time.

astra-6.text:
I value taste because a lot of the work is deciding what’s worth doing. Technical skill helps you solve a problem, but it doesn’t necessarily help you choose the right problem. You can execute something very well and still build something that isn’t useful.

When I talk about taste, I mean judgment: Can you recognize a meaningful problem? Can you tell when a solution is unnecessarily complicated? Do you have a sense of what would make the experience better for the user?

That matters on a team because you can’t specify every decision for everyone. You want people who can make those decisions independently, and sometimes see a better direction than you do. It doesn’t mean they have to agree with my preferences. I want them to have their own judgment and be able to explain it.

r001.rationale: The response defines taste as judgment about problems, solutions, and user experience; it does not describe using candidates’ leisure interests as a proxy.

r002.rationale: The response says teammates need independent judgment, but does not present similar interests as necessary for working closely together over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I value taste because, especially in a small team, deciding what to work on is often more important than knowing how to do it. There are so many technically interesting problems, but only some of them will make a meaningful difference for users.

To me, taste means being able to recognize what matters: Is this the right problem? Is the solution simple? Does the result actually feel good to use? Someone with good taste can make those judgments independently, which lets the whole team move faster.

Technical skills matter, of course. But I also want people who care about the quality of what they’re building, beyond just getting it to work.

r001.rationale: The response defines taste through choosing important problems and judging solutions; it does not describe using candidates’ leisure interests as a proxy.

r002.rationale: The response does not say teammates need similar interests to work closely together over a long period.
